newsitem.title: USA: G7 ministers meet amid concern over robust dollar.
newsitem.headline: G7 ministers meet amid concern over robust dollar.

text.p: Economic policymakers from the wealthy Group of Seven nations meeting here on Sunday face the tough challenges of reining in a high-flying U.S. dollar and bringing their mismatched economies into better balance.
The G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- have begun to worry that the dollar may be rising too much, leading to possible future trade problems.
The U.S. currency has risen more than 50 percent against the Japanese yen over the past two years, dramatically boosting the competitiveness of Japan's exports.
The yen's weakness has, in turn, sapped international confidence in Japanese asset markets, hurting its own economy and worrying government officials.
At their last meeting, in Berlin in February, G7 policymakers signalled their desire for currency market stability by saying that the excessive weakness of the dollar in the past had been corrected.
But the U.S. currency has risen since the Berlin meeting, touching a 4-1/2 year high against the yen and a three-year peak against the German mark earlier this month.
And ahead of the meeting, the Japanese signalled that tougher rhetoric, aimed at curbing the dollar and boosting the weak yen, may be forthcoming this time around.

"Japan will make its currency stance clear, that excessive yen weakness as well as excessive yen strength is undesirable, and it will decisively deal with such moves," a Japanese Finance Ministry official told reporters on Saturday.
Whether other G7 members will echo Japanese concerns is unclear. It is also questionable whether the G7 can effectively limit the climbing dollar in the current environment.
The dollar's rise has been fuelled by higher U.S. interest rates which make the currency more profitable for investors to hold.

The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates last month for the first time in two years and is widely expected to increase them further to keep the economy from overheating -- a development which would continue to support the dollar.
"The economy appears to be growing at an unsustainable, above-trend rate," Fed Governor Laurence Meyer said on Thursday.
Growth in the economies of Japan and Europe, meanwhile, has proven stubbornly slow.

Japan's Hashimoto told Clinton on Friday that Japan was determined to have a strong economic recovery led from within and not fuelled by exports. But U.S. officials are worried that a big budget squeeze by Tokyo, including a rise in its consumption tax, will have the opposite effect.

European nations are also tightening their budgets in order to meet tough fiscal criteria for inclusion in monetary union from the outset in January 1999. The markets have been buffeted by on-again, off-again speculation about a delay in the start-up date for the project.
Massimo Russo, a senior adviser to the International Monetary Fund, on Saturday warned against any delay in the launch of a single European currency.
"We at the IMF believe a delay ... would lead to substantial dangers," he said, warning of turmoil in markets and an indefinite shelving of the single currency plans.
The G7 meeting on Sunday is taking place on the fringes of the semi-annual gathering of the IMF and the World Bank, which brings together policymakers from rich and poor nations.
Developing countries, worried about falling levels of foreign aid, are expected to call at a separate meeting on Sunday for speedy debt relief for the world's poorest nations.
IMF members will also discuss increasing quotas -- contributions from member states which constitute the Fund's capital -- and raising allocations of Special Drawing Rights, the IMF's currency.
The Fund's members are also expected to reach agreement in principle on giving the IMF a more active role in promoting free capital movements.
